content:
Hello all,

I asked in the mathlib community meeting whether textbooks for 1st-year math PhD students had been formalized.I was told to ask here and be more specific. What I had in mind was based on my own previous studies. So, I'll say a little about how I studied math in order to explain which textbooks I'm thinking of and why. I'll put all the textbooks on separate lines so you can easily skip the backstory. Of course, the same material may have been covered by formalizations of different textbooks. I'm looking for one where (at least some of) the material is not already in mathlib. I have in mind to take up the textbook formalization while learning Lean, and hopefully make contributions to mathlib along the way.

I got my bachelor's in (pure) math from Caltech and my PhD in pure math from UC Berkeley (and got an MS in CS from UC Berkeley along the way). As an undergrad, I elected to take complex analysis, based on:

Lars Ahlfors, Complex Analysis

I mention it here because Berkeley required incoming PhD students to immediately take a preliminary exam, which included complex analysis. Some of my fellow grad students didn't pass on their first attempt, since complex analysis had not been required during their math majors (as it wasn't in mine). I passed my prelim on the first attempt and didn't take complex analysis as a 1st-year PhD student, but many people did.

In my senior year of undergrad I took the 1st-year graduate course in algebra at Caltech, based on

Thomas W. Hungerford, Algebra

So I didn't need to take it at Berkeley (I think they might have used Lang there). The 1st-year graduate course that I was required to take at Berkeley was "Introduction to Topology and Analysis", and had these two required textbooks:

John L. Kelley, General Topology

Paul Halmos, Measure Theory

Looking at my transcript, I see that I also took the graduate course "Ordinary and Partial Differential Equations" in my first year. I believe this course was not required. Anyway, I recall that these two were required textbooks:

Earl A. Coddington & Norman Levinson, Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations

E. C. Zachmanoglou & Dale W. Thoe, Introduction to Partial Differential Equations with Applications

As far as I recall, these two textbooks were only recommended:

Vladimir I. Arnold, Ordinary Differential Equations

Fritz John, Partial Differential Equations

I took Differentiable Manifolds in my first year too. That course was not required. If I recall correctly, we used the following textbook in an undergraduate course at Caltech. I'm just putting it here as I was quite fond of it:

Michael Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds

As far as I recall, what we actually used in the graduate course at Berkeley was

Victor Guillemin & Alan Pollack, Differential Topology

So, which of these have already been formalized? And for which of these is the material already covered in mathlib (though possibly not due to a formalization of that specific text)? I was not that fond of Coddington & Levinson. (I think we only used it to get to the theorem on existence and uniqueness of solutions.) My favorite textbook from undergrad was

I. N. Herstein, Topics in Algebra

I presume that material is in mathlib already though.

Thank you,
Ruchira

Well you're asking about ten different questions here, and each of the questions has ten subquestions. So it's difficult to give you a coherent answer.

Broadly speaking we have very little of the diff geom side of things (e.g. Spivak), lots of the algebra side of things (e.g. I should think we have most of Hungerford right now), lots of general topology, lots of measure theory etc etc.

I think you might be better off searching for specific topics yourself. The answer to "is a random grad level thing there" is "sometimes yes, sometimes no". To get a feeling for what is there you might want to go to one of the semantic search engines e.g.

https://leandex.projectnumina.ai/

https://www.leanexplore.com/

https://leansearch.net/

and just get searching.

Thanks for your reply, Kevin. Then it sounds like we already have most of what was required for all Berkeley math PhDs. I'll search for topics of more interest to me personally. It sounds like Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, may be a good choice (I'll search for the material).

Thanks,
Ruchira
Or, I might pick something closer to my subsequent interests. I'll think about it....
It's always more fun to formalise stuff you're mathematically interested in!

One thing that has not been done (to my knowledge, which is very limited) is to compare the body of Mathlib lemmas and definitions and map them to chapters in standard beginning graduate textbooks. The assessments I've seen have the character "this looks like a formalization of things I saw when I read the textbook, so probably most of the textbook is already covered", not "I went through the index and the table of contents, and can map this repository to (the contents of) these specific sections of this specific edition of this specific text". It would be a good way to compare material between different graduate texts on the same topic, something like "Munkres Topology is great when you want to handle these concepts in algebraic topology, but uniform spaces are better covered in Willard's text". Even if all you did was a mapping between a specific text and a specific Mathlib version, it would help encapsulate the body of knowledge covered by that specific text and determine what concepts/results from that text still needed formalizing.
